Not every use of a deserialization library function may be vulnerable, say we
want implement a function "Deserialize" using "JavaScriptSerializer" to
deserialize a "Person" object, provided as a string
an attacker may be able to control the instantiation of the object's Serializer.
If the SimpleTypeResolver is used when instantiating a JavaScriptSerializer,
then the subsequent deserialization will be susceptible to exploitation.
Or a combination of gadgets called a gadget chain, is an object set up in a specific way so that it executes a desired set of actions upon
deserialization, most importantly, in the context of attacks we want to carry out.
The ObjectDataProvider class is part of the Windows Presentation Foundation, which is a .NET framework for developing graphic user interfaces
When we deserialize an object in .NET we can't execute any functions, Except that ObjectDataProvider does so automatically !
ObjectDataProvider has the following fields (among others):
ObjectType: Used to set the type of object to create an instance of
MethodName: Set the name of a method to call when creating the object
MethodParameters: The list of parameters to be passed to the method
using just these three fields, we should be able to create an instance of an arbitrary object, and call an arbitrary method with arbitrary
parameters, all without invoking a single method.
This example in C# uses ObjectDataProvider to create an instance of
System.Diagnostics.Process and invokes the Start method with parameters
We can search for more serializer-specific vulns,
for example, checking which value of TypeNameHandling
Json.NET is used, non-None value = potentially vulnerable
For XmlSerializer, the condition is you have to be in control
of the type, for example if it's controlled client side in
hidden input html tag in form
For BinaryFormatter, it's explicitely mentione on
microsoft's documentation that it's vulnerable and
should not be used, there's no particulare condition
for exploitation, just choosing the right gadget chain
